Instead, Source [S2] discusses 'Neural Radiance Caching' (Müller et al. 2021) and its use of online learning. The claim conflates 'Neural Surface Caches' with the online learning capabilities typically associated with 'Neural Radiance Caching' or other methods, and incorrectly attributes the online learning aspect to the specific citations for Neural Surface Caches which the text says cannot directly shade unseen dynamic objects without ray tracing and do not inherently support the online learning adaptation described in the second part of the claim in the same way. Furthermore, the citations [RWG*13, HCZ21, CDD*24] are linked to static surface storage, not the online learning adaptation mentioned.

S1 states that Neural Surface Cache 'cannot directly shade objects that are not part of the training domain' and requires 'ray tracing to defer shading computations to the trained static surface locations' to handle dynamic objects. In contrast, S1 claims NIV (the proposed method) achieves higher quality and runs faster because it does *not* require this deferral/ray tracing overhead. Furthermore, Source [S2] describes Neural Radiance Caching as predicting colors from feature buffers, not primarily as a deferral mechanism for indirect illumination in the manner described. The claim conflates the 'deferral' technique (attributed to Neural Surface Cache in S1) with the solution provided by the authors (NIV), which S1 argues avoids the need for such deferral.
